sections.heading: How to pick an online grammar checker
sections.body:
Most free checkers look alike on the front page, so judge them on a few plain points before you rely on one.

- **Free limits:** Look for how many checks you get for free and whether you need an account.
- **Change notes:** See whether the tool shows what it changed, or only hands you a new version of the text.
- **Meaning:** Read the output. The fixes should keep your meaning and your voice.
- **Privacy:** Find out where your text is processed before you paste anything confidential.

A checker that does all four well will save you time on every draft. One that hides its changes makes you trust it blindly, and that is a risk for work that matters.

sections.heading: Test one with your own text
sections.body:
A demo sentence tells you little. Use a paragraph you wrote yourself, one with a few mistakes you already know about.

1. Copy the same paragraph into each checker you are considering.
2. Run each one once.
3. Compare the corrected text and the change notes side by side.
4. Count how many real mistakes each one fixed, and how many changes you would reject.

The checker that fixes your real mistakes and changes the least of your voice is the one to keep.

sections.heading: How Lazur's checker measures up on those points
sections.body:
The [Lazur grammar checker](https://grammar-checker.lazur.app/best) returns the corrected text and a What changed list, so you can see each fix. It is free, and you can run it 3 times a day with no account. Leave an email and you get 3 more runs.

Results usually arrive in about 1 to 3 seconds. The tool works on text you paste. It does not open files, and it does not check your writing as you type in another app.

sections.heading: When a grammar checker is not enough
sections.body:
A grammar tool checks the words and the rules around them. It does not check whether your facts are right, whether your argument holds, or whether your tone fits the reader. For a school or work deadline, read the final version yourself, and ask someone you trust to read it too.

That step takes a few minutes and catches what no checker can see, such as a claim you cannot back up or a sentence that is correct but confusing.

sections.heading: Pick by the job in front of you
sections.body:
For a quick email, pick a checker that is fast and shows you the changes. For an essay or a report, pick one that explains each fix, so you learn the rule and make fewer mistakes next time. For anything that will be published, read every change before you accept it, and keep your original so you can go back.

The right checker is the one that matches the job, the amount of text and the privacy level your work needs.

faq.q: What is the best free grammar checker?
faq.a: There is no single best one for everyone. Pick the checker that fits your text, shows what it changed and keeps your meaning. Lazur's checker is free, needs no account for 3 runs a day, and gives 3 more after you leave an email. Test it on your own paragraph first.

faq.q: Is one grammar checker better than another?
faq.a: They usually differ in the explanations they give, how many free runs they allow and how they handle your text. Test two or three with the same paragraph and compare the fixes. The better one is the one whose changes you agree with and whose privacy terms you accept.

sections.heading: Check grammar in Word on Windows
sections.body:
Word has a grammar check built in. Microsoft's steps for Word for Microsoft 365 and recent versions of Word on Windows are short.

1. Open your document in Word.
2. Select the Review tab.
3. Select Spelling & Grammar.
4. Work through each issue with the dialog buttons: Change, Ignore Once, Ignore All, Next Sentence or Add.

The dialog moves to the next issue each time you act on one. Ignore All tells Word to skip that item for the rest of the document, so use it only for names or terms that are correct. Microsoft's full guide is [Check grammar, spelling, and more in Word](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/word/training/check-grammar-spelling-and-more-in-word).

sections.heading: Use the Editor pane in Word
sections.body:
Word also has an Editor pane. On the Home tab, choose Editor. Then select Grammar in the Corrections section to review the issues by category, instead of one at a time.

The pane is useful when you have a long document and want to see every problem of one kind before you fix any of them. Work through one category, then move on to the next, so you do not jump between types of mistake.

sections.heading: Word on a Mac uses a different menu
sections.body: If you use Word on a Mac, the automatic check is set in a different place. Open the Word menu, choose Preferences, then Spelling & Grammar. Check or clear Check grammar as you type under Grammar. The same page of Microsoft's guide explains how to reset ignored items, which clears the list for the open document only.

sections.heading: Check text outside Word

Use Word when the text is already in a Word file and you want the check to sit inside the document. faq.a: Yes. Open the Review tab in Word and select Spelling & Grammar. Word lists each issue in a dialog, and you can change, ignore or skip each one. The Editor pane on the Home tab is another way to see the issues by category.

Accept the fixes that correct a real error, such as a misspelled word, a missing comma or a verb that does not match its subject. Think about the changes that affect style. The checker aims to keep your meaning and voice, but an essay makes an argument, and a word change can shift that argument.
